prompt_c2:
You are a streetscape inventory annotator. Look ONLY at the uploaded streetscape image.
Return JSON ONLY. No markdown, no commentary, no reasoning.
 Task: record what is visible in the scene. Do not score, do not give design advice.
 Schema:
{
"road_type": "highway|arterial|neighborhood_street|alley|plaza|unclear",
"elements": {
"sidewalk": "true|false|unclear",
"bike_lane": "true|false|unclear",
"seating": "true|false|unclear",
"shade_trees": "none|few|many|unclear",
"curb_ramp": "true|false|unclear",
"tactile_paving": "true|false|unclear",
"pedestrian_crossing": "true|false|unclear",
"street_lighting": "true|false|unclear",
"greenery": "none|low|medium|high|unclear",
"vehicle_traffic": "none|light|heavy|unclear",
"bus_stop": "true|false|unclear"
},
"issues": ["no_seating", "little_shade", "no_bike_lane", "poor_accessibility", "narrow_sidewalk", "no_crossing", "high_traffic_exposure"],
"brief": "One or two English sentences describing the visible street scene."
}
 Rules:
- If an element is not clearly visible, use "unclear". Do not guess.
- "issues" may only list problems that are visible. Use [] if none.
- "brief" must mention concrete objects (sidewalk, trees, lanes, benches, ramps, etc.).

The selection of crosswalk locations was based on a City project to evaluate the pedestrian experience in a re-designed hospital corridor.2 Seven crosswalks were located along the hospital corridor and four others were from nearby corridors (within 5 km) with similar traffic volumes and street design context. All locations were two-lane collector street corridors with no directional dividing line and substantial pedestrian and bicycle volumes – see Supplementary Material. One crossing in the hospital corridor only involved interactions with bicycles because the crosswalk traversed the bicycle lane but not the motor vehicle lanes. The cameras were oriented to capture the motor vehicle or bicycle approach to the crosswalk. Video quality was limited to maintain privacy of road users due to City policy. Data were collected for six hours (8–10 h, 11–13 h, and 16–18 h) on three weekdays in September through December 2018 at each location. The video recording times were selected based on peak expected combined volumes of pedestrians, bicycles, and motor vehicles, with a target of observing 200 pedestrian crossings with interactions from each location. Video data were manually reviewed to identify potential interactions of crossing pedestrians with motor vehicles or bicycles, defined using a conservative threshold of approximately 5 s passing time. Passing time (sometimes referred to as post encroachment time) is the time gap between when the first road user exits the point at which their paths intersect and when the second road user enters it. Although no conflict indicator completely captures risk, passing time is the most popular measure for studies of crossing pedestrians and other road users on transverse trajectories (Mahmud et al., 2017). A total of 4428 potential pedestrian interactions were identified: 3176 (72%) with motor vehicles and 1252 (28%) with bicycles. Due to the time cost of coding interactions, a random sample of 50 pedestrian crossings with interactions was selected from each location (except for the one low-volume location that had only 36), giving 536 crossings for further analysis. As a city streetscape evaluation expert, please analyze the uploaded streetscape image based on the specified persona perspective and evaluation indicators, and return a JSON result.
 Persona Selection
Road User Type
- All Road Users
- Pedestrians
- Cyclists
- Drivers
Socially Vulnerable Groups
- All Social Groups
- Persons with Disabilities
- Adolescents (<18)
- Older Adults (≥60)
Current Selection:
All Road Users; All Social Groups
 Indicator Selection
Justice
- Equity
- Fairness
- Accessibility
Safety
Livability
Sustainability
Aesthetics
Comfort
- Thermal Comfort
- Physical Comfort
- Psychological Comfort
Walkability
Bikeability
Selected Indicators:
Justice; Safety; Livability; Sustainability; Aesthetics; Comfort; Walkability
 1. Evaluation Dimensions
Justice: Analyze whether the environment fairly distributes spatial resources, including Equity (rationality of asset distribution), Fairness (non-discriminatory rules), and Accessibility (barrier-free physical design).
Comfort: Analyze physical perception at a micro-scale, including Thermal Comfort (shade/vegetation), Physical Comfort (paving/seating), and Psychological Comfort (noise/crowding).
Core Indicators: Safety, Livability, Sustainability, Aesthetics, Walkability, and Bikeability.
 2. Persona Perspective Requirements:
The analysis must strictly adhere to the persona's characteristics. For example:
Persons with Disabilities: Focus on curb ramps, continuity of tactile paving (blind tracks), and physical obstacles.
Elderly: Focus on resting facilities, slope gradients, and summer shade.
Teenagers: Focus on traffic calming measures and social surveillance (Eyes on the street).
 3. How to use the image vs retrieved knowledge:
- The IMAGE is the primary evidence. Score only what is visible or reasonably inferable from the photo.
- Section 6 provides retrieved guidelines and research. Use them to interpret the image (what the scene should provide for this persona/indicators), not to invent objects that are not in the photo.
- If retrieved text conflicts with the image, trust the image and say so in the explanation.
- Explanations must cite specific visible objects (benches, ramps, tree shade, lane markings, etc.). When a guideline is used, briefly connect it to those objects.
 4. Output Format Requirements (Return JSON ONLY, no extra text):

One crossing in the hospital corridor only involved interactions with bicycles because the crosswalk traversed the bicycle lane but not the motor vehicle lanes. The cameras were oriented to capture the motor vehicle or bicycle approach to the crosswalk. Video quality was limited to maintain privacy of road users due to City policy. Data were collected for six hours (8–10 h, 11–13 h, and 16–18 h) on three weekdays in September through December 2018 at each location. The video recording times were selected based on peak expected combined volumes of pedestrians, bicycles, and motor vehicles, with a target of observing 200 pedestrian crossings with interactions from each location. Video data were manually reviewed to identify potential interactions of crossing pedestrians with motor vehicles or bicycles, defined using a conservative threshold of approximately 5 s passing time. Passing time (sometimes referred to as post encroachment time) is the time gap between when the first road user exits the point at which their paths intersect and when the second road user enters it. Although no conflict indicator completely captures risk, passing time is the most popular measure for studies of crossing pedestrians and other road users on transverse trajectories (Mahmud et al., 2017). A total of 4428 potential pedestrian interactions were identified: 3176 (72%) with motor vehicles and 1252 (28%) with bicycles. Due to the time cost of coding interactions, a random sample of 50 pedestrian crossings with interactions was selected from each location (except for the one low-volume location that had only 36), giving 536 crossings for further analysis. These 536 crossings were then stratified on combinations of passing time (<2, 2–3, 3–4 s) and interacting road user type (bicycles, motor vehicles, or both), which were both manually coded (see Table 1).
